{{Nihongo|'''Leo Esaki'''|江崎 玲於奈|Esaki Reona|born March 12, 1925}} is a Japanese [[physicist]] who shared the 1973 [[Nobel Prize in Physics]] with [[Ivar Giaever]] and [[Brian Josephson]] for his work on [[Quantum tunnelling|tunneling]] in [[semiconductor]]s,<ref name="Nobel Prize">{{Cite web|title=Nobel Prize in Physics 1973|url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1973/summary/|url-status=live|publisher=NobelPrize.org|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110621141041/http://nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/physics/laureates/1973/index.html |archive-date=2011-06-21|access-date=2008-10-09}}</ref> which led to his invention of the [[tunnel diode]] that exploits this phenomenon. His research was done when he was with [[Sony]]. He has also contributed in being a pioneer of semiconductor [[superlattice]]s.

Since the death of [[Yoichiro Nambu]] in 2015, Esaki is the oldest living [[Japanese Nobel laureate]].

== Biography ==
Leo Esaki was born on March 12, 1925, in [[Osaka]], Japan. Esaki studied physics at the [[University of Tokyo]], where he received a [[Bachelor of Science]] in 1947 and a [[Doctor of Philosophy]] in 1959.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Leo Esaki – Biographical |url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1973/esaki/biographical/|url-status=live |publisher=NobelPrize.org|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20250212020111/https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1973/esaki/biographical/|archive-date=2025-02-12|access-date=2025-08-16}}</ref> In 1947, he joined the Kobe Kogyo Corporation, before becoming chief physicist at Tokyo Tsushin Kogyo (now [[Sony]]) in 1956.<ref>{{Cite encyclopedia|title=Leo Esaki |url=https://www.britannica.com/biography/Leo-Esaki|url-status=live|encyclopedia=Encyclopædia Britannica|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20251124040542/https://www.britannica.com/biography/Leo-Esaki|archive-date=2025-11-24|access-date=2025-08-16}}</ref>

In 1960, Esaki moved to the United States to join [[IBM]]'s [[Thomas J. Watson Research Center]], where he was appointed an [[IBM Fellow]] in 1967. In 1992, he returned to Japan, where he subsequently served as President of the [[University of Tsukuba]] until 1998.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Prof. Dr. Leo Esaki – CV|url=https://mediatheque.lindau-nobel.org/laureates/esaki/cv|url-status=live|publisher=Lindau Mediatheque|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260123135844/https://mediatheque.lindau-nobel.org/laureates/esaki/cv|archive-date=2026-01-23|access-date=2026-06-11}}</ref>

== Research ==
=== Tunneling ===
In 1957, Esaki recognized that when the [[p–n junction]] width of [[germanium]] is thinned, the [[current–voltage characteristic]] is dominated by the influence of the [[Quantum tunnelling|tunnel effect]]. As a result, he discovered that as the voltage is increased, the current decreases inversely, indicating [[negative resistance]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Esaki|first=Leo|year=1958|title=New Phenomenon in Narrow Germanium p-n Junctions|url=https://journals.aps.org/pr/abstract/10.1103/PhysRev.109.603|url-access=subscription|journal=[[Physical Review]]|volume=109|issue=2|pages=603–604|bibcode=1958PhRv..109..603E|doi=10.1103/PhysRev.109.603}}</ref> This discovery was the first demonstration of solid tunneling effects in physics, and it was the birth of the first [[Quantum electronics|quantum electronic]] device, the [[tunnel diode]].

=== Superlattices ===
In 1969, Esaki predicted that semiconductor [[superlattices]] will be formed to induce a differential negative-resistance effect via an artificially one-dimensional periodic structural changes in semiconductor crystals.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Esaki|first1=L.|last2=Tsu|first2=R.|author-link2=Raphael Tsu|year=1970|title=Superlattice and Negative Differential Conductivity in Semiconductors|url=https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/5391729|url-access=subscription|journal=[[IBM Journal of Research and Development]]|volume=14|issue=1|pages=61–65|doi=10.1147/rd.141.0061}}</ref> His unique "[[molecular-beam epitaxy]]" thin-film crystal growth method can be regulated quite precisely in ultrahigh vacuum. A 1987 comment by Esaki regarding the original paper notes:
<blockquote>
"The original version of the paper was rejected for publication by ''[[Physical Review]]'' on the referee's unimaginative assertion that it was 'too speculative' and involved 'no new physics.' However, this proposal was quickly accepted by the Army Research Office..."<ref>"This Weeks's Citation Classic", ''[[Current Contents]]'' No 28, July 13, 1987.</ref>
</blockquote>

In 1972, Esaki realized his concept of superlattices in III-V group semiconductors. Later, this concept influenced many fields like metals and magnetic materials.

== Family ==
Esaki's daughter, Anna Esaki, is married to [[Craig S. Smith]], former [[Shanghai]] bureau chief of ''[[The New York Times]]'' and [[China]] bureau chief of ''[[The Wall Street Journal]]''.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Anna Esaki Wed To Craig S. Smith|date=1990-01-14|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1990/01/14/style/anna-esaki-wed-to-craig-s-smith.html|url-access=subscription|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|access-date=2021-08-19}}</ref>

== Esaki's "five don'ts" rules ==
At the 1994 [[Lindau Nobel Laureate Meetings]], Esaki suggested a list of "five don'ts" which anyone in realizing their creative potential should follow. Two months later,  the chairman of the Nobel Committee for Physics [[Carl Nordling]] incorporated the rules in his own speech.<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1088/0031-8949/1995/T59/001|bibcode=1995PhST...59...21N|url=https://web.stanford.edu/~rotundu/documents/how_to_get_it.pdf|title=How to get the Nobel Prize in physics|year=1995|last1=Nordling|first1=Carl|journal=Physica Scripta|volume=59|pages=21–25|s2cid=250817314 }}</ref>
#Don't allow yourself to be trapped by your past experiences.
#Don't allow yourself to become overly attached to any one authority in your field – the great professor, perhaps.
#Don't hold on to what you don't need.
#Don't avoid confrontation.
#Don't forget your spirit of childhood curiosity.

== Commemoration ==
In recognition of three Nobel laureates' contributions, the bronze statues of [[Shin'ichirō Tomonaga]], Leo Esaki, and [[Makoto Kobayashi (physicist)|Makoto Kobayashi]] were set up in the Central Park of Azuma 2 in [[Tsukuba]] in 2015.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://mainichi.jp/feature/news/m20150316ddlk08040111000c.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150424074404/http://mainichi.jp/feature/news/m20150316ddlk08040111000c.html|url-status=dead|title=ノーベル賞:江崎、小林、朝永氏の銅像やレリーフ設置 完成記念式でお披露目 「子どもが夢を」−−つくば・中央公園 ／茨城 - 毎日新聞|archive-date=April 24, 2015|access-date=August 9, 2019}}</ref>
